tagline: Long-running note app for capture, search, tasks, and cross-device notes.
verdictSummary: A personal notes app with tags, attachments, OCR on scanned images, and full-text search is a real weekend build. What doesn't come with it is Evernote's actual moat: years of accumulated notes and switching cost, mature sync across every device, and a browser clipper refined over a decade.
coreLoopDIY: A Markdown notes app with tags, file attachments OCR'd on upload so scans stay searchable, full-text search, and a bookmarklet-based web clipper.
whatYouLose: a polished browser and mobile clipper
import/export edge cases handled over years
the reliability of a product that has outlasted most of its competitors
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay because all their old notes, scans, and clipped pages are already there — the switching cost of years of accumulated data is the real product, not the notes editor itself.
notes: A good example where the core editor is easy but capture depth and years of data are what actually drive retention.
prompt:
Build a personal notes app: Markdown notes with tags, edited with a live preview. Support attachments — dropping a file or image onto a note stores it and links it back; run OCR on uploaded images and PDF pages so scans and receipts become searchable, not just their filenames. Build full-text search across both note content and OCR'd attachment text. Add a simple web-clipper bookmarklet (not a browser extension) that posts the current page's title, URL, and selected text into a new note. Write a one-off importer for Evernote's own export format so existing notes, tags, and attachments actually move in. Support a scheduled export of everything to plain Markdown files plus their attachments, so nothing is ever trapped in the app.

Do not build mobile apps, real-time cross-device sync, or a full browser extension — a bookmarklet and a working import path are the honest, complete scope for a personal capture tool.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Evernote notes?
faq.a: Yes — Evernote exports to its own .enex format, and the prompt includes an importer that reads notes, tags, and attachments from it.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: As a responsive web page, yes, if hosted somewhere reachable, but there's no offline mobile app and no camera-based scan capture the way Evernote's app has.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting and a database, typically a few dollars a month — OCR runs locally at no extra cost.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Years of refined capture. Evernote's web clipper and mobile scanning have been tuned for over a decade to handle edge cases cleanly; a bookmarklet and a basic OCR pass cover the common case, not all of them.
